parts.text: What is the most common cause of bacterial parotitis?

cohort_answer.text: Staph aureus. || Buccal PCR, IgM. || AOM; Aseptic meningitis; Orchitis/oophoritis; Deafness.

questions.question: You see a 15 year-old boy presenting with a 3-day history of bilateral testicular pain. He recently returned from a school trip to East Europe. He had a preceding febrile illness with fever and malaise approximately 3 weeks into his trip. On examination, he has swelling and tenderness of both testes and epididymides. He has some submandibular swelling but no swollen glands.

parts.text: List TWO tests that should be performed to make the diagnosis.

questions.model_answer: Two tests for diagnosis of mumps (orchitis with prior parotid/glandular involvement, unvaccinated exposure risk in Eastern Europe): (1) Mumps-specific IgM serology (and/or paired acute/convalescent IgG showing a rise). (2) RT-PCR (or viral culture) of buccal/oral swab or saliva for mumps virus RNA.

questions.question:
Q42 (2011 AM, 2011 PM, 2008)
Young girl with symptoms of Mumps

cohort_answer.text:
A: Incubation period: 16-18 days (range 12-25). Most Infectious: 2 days before, 5 days after parotitis onset (virus isolated from saliva 7d prior and 9 days after). Symptoms: many subclinical; may have a few days fever, myalgia, malaise, followed by nonsuppurative parotitis within 48h. Complications: orchitis/oophoritis, meningitis/encephalitis, deafness. Self-limited, takes a few weeks to fully recover

B: For parotitis - Bacterial: S aureus, Gram negative organisms (often unilateral swollen gland with overlying erythema, purulent drainage from Stenson's duct with parotid massage, post-op/debilitated patients with poor oral intake, premature infants). Viral: Influenza A, Coxsackie, Parainfluenza (adenovirus, EBV, CMV, LCMV, HSV, HIV) - prodromal phase. Noninfectious: Drugs (bilateral, asymptomatic - Phenylbutazone, thiouracil, iodides); Other: diabetes, malnutrition, cirrhosis, uremia, Sjogrens, tumour, parotid stone

C: RT-PCR: buccal/oral swab, serum, urine, CSF. PHOL: do both urine and buccal. Can also send for culture. Serology: positive IgM - may not be positive until 5 days after onset of symptoms, remains positive for 4 weeks, repeat IgM in 5-10 days if negative. Serologic tests cannot differentiate between vaccination and prior mumps exposure, and the level of mumps IgG antibody needed for protection is not known

D: Orchitis/Oophoritis (5-10d after onset of parotitis), Aseptic meningitis, Encephalitis, Deafness (acute onset), Myocarditis, Thyroiditis, Pancreatitis, Interstitial nephritis, Arthritis

E: Mumps vaccination and IG in non-immune exposed individuals does not alter course of disease if it develops. However, recommend vaccination of susceptible individuals as this will protect against future exposures. Born after 1970 and received <2 doses of MMR (age varies by province), no laboratory-confirmed mumps, no documented immunity. Efficacy of vaccine: 60-90% with 1 dose, 75-95% with 2 doses; immunity wanes over time. NB: Mumps occurs even in fully vaccinated adults, although vaccination limits size, duration, and spread of outbreaks.

F: Family: Paramyxoviridae, Genus: Rubulavirus, Species: Mumps rubulavirus

questions.question: In the following table, fill out if the virus is RNA/DNA, and whether it is enveloped or not. For each virus, name one antiviral that has activity against it, if any (Mumps is given as an example). Table columns: Virus, RNA or DNA, Enveloped (Yes or No), Antiviral. Viruses listed: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Influenza, Zika, Ebola.

parts.text: Fill out the table for RNA/DNA, enveloped status, and antiviral for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Influenza, Zika, Ebola

questions.model_answer: Mumps (example): ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care). Measles: ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care; ribavirin used off-label in severe cases). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded DNA, enveloped; antivirals - tenofovir or entecavir. EBV: double-stranded DNA, enveloped; no specific approved antiviral (ganciclovir/valganciclovir used off-label for select EBV-driven disease). Influenza: ssRNA (negative-sense, segmented), enveloped; antivirals - oseltamivir (or zanamivir, baloxavir). Zika: ssRNA (positive-sense), enveloped; no approved antiviral. Ebola: ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; antivirals - monoclonal antibody therapies (e.g., ansuvimab, atoltivimab/maftivimab/odesivimab); remdesivir has also been studied.

parts.text: Complete the table (Nucleic Acid, Envelope, Antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Ebola, Zika

questions.model_answer: Mumps: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care only). Measles: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care; ribavirin has been used off-label in severe cases). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded DNA, enveloped; antivirals - tenofovir, entecavir (also lamivudine/adefovir/telbivudine). EBV: double-stranded DNA, enveloped; no specific approved antiviral for routine infection (ganciclovir/valganciclovir used off-label for select EBV-driven disease). Ebola virus: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; antivirals - monoclonal antibody cocktails (e.g., REGN-EB3/inmazeb, ansuvimab) and remdesivir has been studied. Zika virus: single-stranded positive-sense RNA, enveloped; no approved antiviral (supportive care only).
